title: Python Interview Practice — OOP
topics: Understand classes as blueprints and objects as instances.
Initialize object state with the constructor.
Work with per-object data and behavior.
Control access to object state and understand naming conventions.
Reuse and extend behavior with parent and child classes.
Use a common interface with different implementations.
Combine OOP concepts with Python collections, functions and interview traps.

questions.q: What is a class in Python?
hints: A class defines structure and behavior.
Objects are created from classes.
Think of a class as a blueprint.

questions.q: What is an object?
hints: Car is the class.
c is created by calling Car().
An instance is another name for an object created from a class.

questions.q: Create a class named Student and create one object named s.
questions.expected: Use class Student: pass and then s = Student().
hints: A class definition starts with class.
An empty class can use pass.
Create the object by calling the class.

questions.q: What is printed?
hints: d is an instance of Dog.
type(d) gives its class.
The class name is Dog.

questions.q: Create a class Calculator with a method add(a,b) that returns a+b.
questions.expected: Define Calculator and an instance method add(self,a,b) returning a+b.
hints: Methods inside classes normally receive self first.
add needs two additional parameters.
Use return a+b.

questions.q: How do you access an object's attribute?
hints: Python uses dot notation for normal attribute access.
The object name comes first.
The attribute name follows a dot.

questions.q: Create a class Person and give an object p a name attribute with value 'Ravi'.
questions.expected: Use class Person: pass; p=Person(); p.name='Ravi'.
hints: Create the class first.
Instantiate it.
Assign the attribute with dot notation.

questions.q: What does self usually refer to?
hints: Instance methods receive the current object.
self is the conventional parameter name.
It lets the method access instance attributes and other methods.

questions.q: When is __init__ normally called?
hints: Calling Person() creates an instance.
Python then invokes initialization logic.
__init__ is commonly used to set initial state.

questions.q: Create a Person class whose __init__ stores name in self.name.
questions.expected: Use def __init__(self,name): self.name=name.
hints: The constructor method is __init__.
Store the parameter on the instance.
Use self.name = name.

questions.q: What is printed?
questions.code:
class A:
    def __init__(self,x): self.x=x
a=A(5)
print(a.x)
hints: 5 is passed into x.
self.x stores that value on the object.
a.x retrieves it.

questions.q: Create a Book class with title and price initialized by __init__.
questions.expected: Use __init__(self,title,price) and assign self.title and self.price.
hints: Create two parameters.
Store both on self.
Use dot attributes.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of __init__?
hints: It runs during instance creation.
It commonly assigns initial attributes.
It is not the destructor.

questions.q: Create an Employee class with name='Unknown' as a default constructor argument.
questions.expected: Use def __init__(self,name='Unknown'): self.name=name.
hints: Defaults work like normal function parameters.
self is still the first parameter.
Store the selected name.

questions.q: Which statement is true?
hints: The class exists before instances are made.
Initialization happens for an instance.
A normal __init__ must return None.

questions.q: Which attribute is normally specific to each object?
hints: self attributes belong to an instance.
Two Dog objects can have different names.
Class attributes are shared differently.

questions.q: Create a BankAccount with balance initialized to 0 and a deposit(amount) method that adds to balance.
questions.expected: Use self.balance=0 and self.balance += amount.
hints: Initialize balance in __init__.
deposit receives self and amount.
Modify the instance attribute.

questions.q: What is printed?
questions.code:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self): self.n=0
    def inc(self): self.n+=1
c=Counter(); c.inc(); c.inc(); print(c.n)
hints: n starts at zero.
Each inc call adds one.
There are two calls.

questions.q: Write a Rectangle class with area() returning self.width*self.height.
questions.expected: Define __init__(self,width,height) and area(self) returning the product.
hints: Store width and height on self.
area needs only self.
Multiply the two attributes.

questions.q: Why is self required in an instance method definition?
options: It represents the current instance and gives access to its state
hints: The method needs a reference to the object.
Python passes the instance when called through an object.
The conventional name is self.

questions.q: Create a Student class with marks and a method average() for three marks.
questions.expected: Store three marks and return their sum divided by 3.
hints: Store the marks as instance attributes.
Use (a+b+c)/3.
Return the calculated value.

questions.q: Where is a class variable normally defined?
hints: company is aligned with the class body.
It is not prefixed with self.
Instances can access it unless shadowed.

questions.q: What is printed?
questions.code:
class A:
    count=0
x=A(); y=A()
print(x.count, y.count)
hints: count is a class attribute.
Neither object changes it here.
Both instances can read the same class value.

questions.q: Create a class Product with a class variable tax_rate=0.18.
questions.expected: Define class Product: tax_rate=0.18.
hints: Put the variable in the class body.
Do not put it inside __init__ for this question.
Use the decimal 0.18.

questions.q: Which decorator creates a class method?
hints: Python provides a built-in decorator for class methods.
It is written with @.
The method receives cls conventionally.

questions.q: Create a class method from_name(cls,name) that returns cls(name).
questions.expected: Use @classmethod and return cls(name).
hints: The decorator is @classmethod.
The first parameter conventionally is cls.
Calling cls creates an instance of the class.

questions.q: What does cls refer to in a class method?
hints: Compare cls with self.
A class method receives the class as its first argument.
It can access class-level state.

questions.q: Create a class Employee with class variable count and increment it in __init__ each time an object is created.
questions.expected: Use Employee.count += 1 or type(self).count += 1 in __init__.
hints: Initialize count before object creation.
Increment once per constructor call.
The counter belongs to the class.

questions.q: Which decorator defines a static method?
hints: It is a standard Python decorator.
A static method does not receive self or cls automatically.
Use @staticmethod.

questions.q: Create a static method is_even(n) returning True when n is even.
questions.expected: Use @staticmethod and return n % 2 == 0.
hints: No self is needed.
Use modulo.
Return the boolean expression.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a static method?
options: It receives no implicit instance/class first argument
hints: Unlike instance/class methods, no implicit object/class is passed.
It can still receive explicit parameters.
It is often used for utility logic related to the class.

questions.q: Create a Temperature class with static method c_to_f(c) returning c*9/5+32.
questions.expected: Use @staticmethod and return c*9/5+32.
hints: The conversion does not require object state.
Make it static.
Use the formula exactly.

questions.q: When is a static method a good choice?
options: When behavior needs neither instance nor class state
hints: Ask whether self or cls is needed.
If neither is required, a static method may fit.
It acts like a namespaced utility function.

questions.q: What does a leading underscore in _balance conventionally communicate?
options: Python makes it impossible to access
It is intended as an internal implementation detail
hints: A single underscore is a convention, not strict enforcement.
It signals internal use.
The attribute can still be accessed.

questions.q: What does __name trigger in Python classes?
hints: Double leading underscores have special behavior.
Python mangles the attribute name with the class name.
This reduces accidental name collisions.

questions.q: Create a Person class with a private-looking __age attribute and a get_age() method.
questions.expected: Assign self.__age in __init__ and return it from get_age().
hints: Use two leading underscores for the requested attribute.
The getter is a normal instance method.
Return the stored value.

questions.q: Which is true about Python private attributes?
options: Double underscore attributes are name-mangled, not truly private
hints: Python does not enforce Java-style private access.
Name mangling changes the attribute's internal name.
It mainly prevents accidental clashes.

questions.q: Create a BankAccount with __balance and deposit/withdraw methods that prevent withdrawal if amount exceeds balance.
questions.expected: Check if amount <= self.__balance before subtracting.
hints: Keep balance behind __balance.
Use a condition before changing it.
Only subtract when sufficient funds exist.

questions.q: What is inheritance used for?
options: Reusing and extending behavior from a parent class
hints: A child class can inherit methods and attributes.
It can also override behavior.
This supports code reuse and specialization.

questions.q: Create Animal with speak() and Dog(Animal) that inherits it.
questions.expected: Define class Dog(Animal): pass after defining Animal.
hints: Define the parent first.
Put the parent name in parentheses.
pass is enough for inheritance here.

questions.q: What does super() commonly help you do?
hints: super() provides a proxy for parent/superclass access.
It is often used to call a parent's __init__.
It is especially useful in inheritance chains.

questions.q: Create Vehicle with __init__(brand), then Car(Vehicle) with an extra model attribute and use super().__init__.
questions.expected: Car.__init__ should call super().__init__(brand) and set self.model=model.
hints: Call the parent initializer first.
Use super().__init__(brand).
Then initialize the child-specific attribute.

questions.q: If a child class defines a method with the same name as the parent, what is this commonly called?
hints: The child supplies its own implementation.
The method name remains the same.
This is method overriding.

questions.q: Create Shape with area() raising NotImplementedError and Circle(Shape) overriding area().
questions.expected: Circle.area should return 3.14*self.radius**2.
hints: The child should replace the parent behavior.
Store radius in the child.
Use radius squared multiplied by pi approximation.

questions.q: What is polymorphism in OOP?
options: One interface can work with objects having different implementations
hints: Think 'many forms'.
Different classes can implement the same method name.
Caller code can often use the common interface.

questions.q: Create Dog and Cat classes, each with speak(), then loop through [Dog(),Cat()] and call speak().
questions.expected: Both classes implement speak(); iterate over the objects and call animal.speak().
hints: Give both classes the same method name.
Store instances in one list.
The loop does not need to check the concrete class.

questions.q: What is duck typing in Python?
options: Objects are usable based on supported behavior rather than declared type
hints: Python often focuses on what an object can do.
If an object provides the required method, code can use it.
An explicit shared parent is not always necessary.

questions.q: Write a function make_speak(animal) that calls animal.speak().
questions.expected: Define make_speak(animal): return animal.speak().
hints: The function should not check type.
Call the common method.
Return its result if the method returns one.

questions.q: Which concept is demonstrated when the same area() call works for Circle and Rectangle objects?
hints: Both objects expose area().
The implementations can differ.
The common call is the key idea.

questions.q: Which module provides tools for defining abstract base classes?
hints: Python's abstract base class support is in a short-named standard module.
It includes ABC and abstractmethod.
The module name is abc.

questions.q: Which decorator marks a method as abstract?
hints: Import it from abc.
It marks methods subclasses are expected to implement.
The decorator name contains 'method'.

questions.q: Create an abstract Shape with abstract area() and a Square subclass implementing it.
questions.expected: Use from abc import ABC, abstractmethod; class Shape(ABC); decorate area with @abstractmethod.
hints: Subclass ABC.
Use @abstractmethod above area.
Square must implement area to be concrete.

questions.q: What is a key benefit of abstraction?
options: Expose necessary interface while hiding implementation details
hints: Users of an abstraction focus on what it does.
Implementation can vary behind the interface.
It is about design and separation of concerns.

questions.q: Design an abstract Payment class with pay(amount), then implement CardPayment.pay().
questions.expected: Payment inherits ABC and pay is abstract; CardPayment implements pay.
hints: Use abc.
Define the required interface in Payment.
Implement the concrete behavior in CardPayment.

questions.q: What is method resolution order (MRO)?
options: The order Python searches classes for attributes/methods
hints: Inheritance can form chains and multiple inheritance.
Python needs a deterministic lookup order.
ClassName.mro() exposes it.

questions.q: What does isinstance(obj, Class) check?
options: Whether obj is an instance of Class or its subclasses
hints: It checks object/class relationship.
Subclass instances can also satisfy the check.
It returns a boolean.

questions.q: Create a class with __str__ returning a user-friendly representation such as 'Student: Ravi'.
questions.expected: Implement def __str__(self): return 'Student: ' + self.name.
hints: __str__ controls the informal string representation.
Return a string, not print it.
Use self.name.

questions.q: What is the difference between __str__ and __repr__ at a high level?
options: __str__ is user-friendly; __repr__ aims for developer/debug representation
hints: Think user-facing vs developer-facing representation.
Both are special methods.
The exact fallback behavior is a useful interview detail.

questions.q: Create a class Point with __eq__ comparing x and y values between two Point objects.
questions.expected: Return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y.
hints: Compare corresponding coordinates.
Return one boolean expression.
Store x and y during initialization.

questions.q: What does @property allow you to do?
options: Expose method-based logic through attribute-style access
Turn a class into a list
hints: A property is accessed without parentheses.
It can compute or validate a value.
It is commonly used for controlled attribute access.

questions.q: Create a Circle class with radius and a read-only @property area.
questions.expected: Define @property def area(self): return 3.14*self.radius**2.
hints: Use @property above area.
Access should look like circle.area.
No setter is required for a read-only property.

questions.q: What is composition?
options: Building a class using objects of other classes
hints: A 'has-a' relationship often suggests composition.
Objects become components of a larger object.
It can reduce tight inheritance coupling.

questions.q: Create Engine with start(), then Car containing an Engine object and a start() method delegating to engine.start().
questions.expected: Initialize self.engine=Engine() and return/call self.engine.start().
hints: Car has an Engine.
Instantiate Engine inside or inject it.
Delegate the behavior to the component.

questions.q: What is printed?
questions.code:
class A:
    x=10
a=A(); a.x=20
print(A.x,a.x)
hints: The assignment a.x creates/shadows an instance attribute.
The class attribute remains 10.
Reading a.x finds the instance attribute first.

questions.q: What is printed?
questions.code:
class A:
    def __init__(self): self.x=[]
a=A(); b=A(); a.x.append(1)
print(b.x)
hints: Each __init__ creates a new list.
The lists belong to separate instances.
Only a.x was modified.

questions.q: What is printed?
questions.code:
class A:
    count=0
    def __init__(self): A.count+=1
A(); A(); print(A.count)
hints: The class variable starts at zero.
Each constructor increments it.
There are two instances.

questions.q: Which relationship best matches inheritance?
hints: A Dog is an Animal is the classic example.
Composition is often described as has-a.
Inheritance models specialization.

questions.q: A function calls obj.draw() without checking whether obj is Circle or Square. What concept is this closest to?
hints: The caller relies on a common behavior.
Concrete object type is not required for the call.
This is a common Python polymorphism pattern.

questions.q: Which is the safest statement about _name?
options: It is a convention indicating internal use
hints: A single underscore does not enforce privacy.
It communicates intent to programmers.
Python conventions matter in API design.

questions.q: Can a static method access instance state through self automatically?
hints: Static methods receive no implicit self.
They need an explicit object passed if they need instance data.
That is a key distinction from instance methods.

questions.q: Can you normally instantiate a class with unimplemented abstract methods?
options: No, Python prevents instantiation of an abstract class
hints: An ABC with abstract methods remains abstract.
Python raises TypeError when trying to instantiate it until required methods are implemented.
Concrete subclasses can then be instantiated.

questions.q: What does super() in a single-inheritance child constructor commonly accomplish?
options: Calls parent implementation without manually naming the parent
hints: super() gives access to the next class in MRO.
Calling super().__init__ initializes inherited state.
It also supports cooperative multiple inheritance patterns.

questions.q: Which is usually preferable when you need to reuse behavior but the relationship is not naturally 'is-a'?
hints: Composition models 'has-a' or collaboration.
It can keep components loosely coupled.
Inheritance is strongest for genuine subtype relationships.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
topicQuestions.code:
class Dog:
    pass
d = Dog()
print(type(d))
hints: type() reports the full class path including the module.
d is an instance of Dog defined in the main module.
The output shows <class '__main__.Dog'>.

topicQuestions.question: Which correctly creates an instance of a class Car?
topicQuestions.code:
class Car:
    pass
hints: Python does not use a 'new' keyword.
Calling the class name like a function creates an instance.
my_car = Car() is correct.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
topicQuestions.code:
class A:
    pass
a1 = A()
a2 = A()
print(a1 is a2)
hints: Each call to A() creates a brand-new object.
a1 and a2 are two separate instances in memory.
is checks identity, so this is False.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
hints: __init__ runs automatically when Person('Sam') is called.
It stores 'Sam' into self.name.
print(p.name) shows Sam without quotes.

topicQuestions.question: When is __init__ automatically called?
options: Whenever a new instance is created
Only when you call it manually
Every time a method is called
hints: __init__ is Python's initializer method.
It runs as part of creating a new object.
ClassName(...) automatically triggers __init__.

topicQuestions.question: What happens if __init__ is defined without self as its first parameter?
hints: Python automatically passes the new instance as the first argument.
Without a parameter to receive it, there's an argument count mismatch.
This raises TypeError: __init__() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
hints: bark() uses self.name to build the message.
self.name is 'Rex' for this instance.
print() displays the text without quotes: Rex says woof.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
hints: Instance attributes can be reassigned after creation.
a.x = 5 overwrites the original value.
print(a.x) shows 5.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
topicQuestions.code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 1
a1 = A()
a2 = A()
a1.x = 99
print(a2.x)
hints: Each instance has its own independent copy of instance attributes.
Changing a1.x does not affect a2.x.
a2.x remains 1.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
topicQuestions.code:
class A:
    count = 0
a1 = A()
a2 = A()
print(A.count)
hints: count is a class variable shared by all instances.
Nothing in this code changes count.
A.count remains 0.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
topicQuestions.code:
class A:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self):
        A.count += 1
a1 = A()
a2 = A()
print(A.count)
hints: Each call to __init__ increments the shared class variable.
Two instances were created, so __init__ ran twice.
A.count becomes 2.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
hints: @classmethod passes the class itself as the first argument, cls.
cls.x refers to the class variable x.
get_x() returns 1.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
hints: A static method behaves like a plain function inside the class.
It doesn't receive self or cls automatically.
MathUtil.add(2, 3) returns 2 + 3 = 5.

topicQuestions.question: Which decorator marks a method that doesn't need access to self or cls?
hints: This decorator is for utility-style methods related to the class.
Such methods don't need instance or class data.
That decorator is @staticmethod.

topicQuestions.question: Can a static method directly access instance attributes?
options: No, because it has no access to self
Only if the class has one instance
hints: Static methods don't receive self as a parameter.
Without self, there's no reference to any particular instance.
So they cannot directly access instance attributes.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?

It signals 'internal use' but doesn't enforce access restrictions.
A()._x is still directly accessible and prints 1.

a._A__x prints 1.

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
hints: Dog inherits speak() from Animal since it doesn't define its own.
Calling Dog().speak() runs Animal's version.
The output is generic sound (no quotes from print).

topicQuestions.question: What is printed?
